steps.body:
L'Hôpital speaks only two languages: **0/0** and **∞/∞**.

But other forms are indeterminate too — 0·∞, ∞ − ∞, 1^∞ — and every one of them can be **rewritten as a quotient**, and then handed over.

The skill is not the rule. It is the rewriting.

explanationVariants: As x → ∞, x/eˣ is ∞/∞. Differentiate top and bottom: 1/eˣ → 0. The exponential wins outright.
The rule applies to ∞/∞ verbatim — no modification at all.

widget.prompt: lim(x→∞) x/eˣ. Apply L'Hôpital and give the value.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the ratio of the leading coefficients, which is not how limits at infinity work here. After differentiating you have 1/eˣ, and eˣ runs away — so the limit is 0.
The limit is a specific number: 1/eˣ → 0 as x grows without bound.

explanationVariants: x·ln x as x → 0⁺ is 0·(−∞). Rewrite as (ln x)/(1/x), which is −∞/∞ — and now the rule applies.
Any factor can be pushed into the denominator as its reciprocal. That is the whole trick.

widget.prompt: lim(x→0⁺) x·ln x is the indeterminate form 0·(−∞). How do you make L'Hôpital applicable?

options.label: Rewrite as (ln x)/(1/x).
options.feedback: Right. Pushing one factor downstairs as its reciprocal turns a product into a quotient, and quotients are the rule's native language.

options.label: Differentiate x·ln x directly.
options.feedback: The rule is stated for QUOTIENTS. There is no bottom to differentiate, so the move is not even defined.

options.label: Conclude 0 from the factor x.
options.feedback: That is precisely what 'indeterminate' rules out: zero times something unbounded can come out as anything. It must be resolved, not assumed.

options.label: Conclude −∞ from the factor ln x.
options.feedback: The other factor is racing to zero at the same time, and which one wins is the entire question. (It is the x — the limit is 0.)

widget.prompt: A hierarchy of growth, settled by L'Hôpital.

panels.title: Exponentials beat polynomials
panels.body: x/eˣ → 0. So does x¹⁰⁰/eˣ: apply the rule a hundred times and the polynomial is ground down to a constant while eˣ sits there unchanged. NO power of x can outrun an exponential.

panels.title: Polynomials beat logarithms
panels.body: (ln x)/x → 0. The logarithm rises forever, but so slowly that even x beats it — and so does √x, and so does x^0.001.

panels.title: The hierarchy
panels.body: ln x ≪ any power of x ≪ eˣ. That one line explains why an algorithm running in log time is fast, why one running in exponential time is hopeless, and why the two are not remotely close.

widget.continueFeedback: Keep going — the third panel is the sentence worth keeping.
widget.successFeedback: ln x ≪ xⁿ ≪ eˣ. L'Hôpital does not merely compute limits; it RANKS the functions.

steps.body:
For **∞ − ∞**, put it over a common denominator. For **1^∞**, take logarithms — the log turns an exponent into a product, and the product into a quotient.

In every case the move is the same: **manufacture a quotient**, check the form, then differentiate.

A narrow tool with a wide reach — and the reach is entirely in the rewriting.

explanationVariants: Exponentials beat every power of x, which beats every logarithm: ln x ≪ x³ ≪ eˣ.
L'Hôpital proves each comparison — differentiate until one side is ground away.

widget.prompt: Order these from SLOWEST-growing to FASTEST, as x → ∞.

misorderFeedback.feedback: eˣ is the fastest of the three. Apply L'Hôpital to x³/eˣ and watch the polynomial get ground down to nothing while eˣ survives untouched.
ln x is the slowest — it is beaten even by √x, let alone by x³.

widget.missFeedback: ln x ≪ any power of x ≪ eˣ.
widget.successFeedback: Logarithms crawl, powers walk, exponentials sprint — and L'Hôpital is what proves it.

hints: The form is 0·(−∞), so manufacture a quotient: (ln x)/(1/x).
That is −∞/∞. Differentiate top and bottom: (1/x)/(−1/x²).
Simplify the compound fraction: (1/x)·(−x²) = −x. Now let x → 0⁺.
explanationVariants: The x wins: it reaches zero faster than ln x reaches −∞. Nothing but the rule could have told you which.

widget.prompt: lim(x→0⁺) x·ln x. Give the value.

commonErrors.feedback: Rewrite as (ln x)/(1/x) and apply the rule: it simplifies to −x, which goes to 0.
It does not run away to a negative value — the x crushes the logarithm, and the limit is exactly 0.

takeaways: The rule speaks only 0/0 and ∞/∞. Every other indeterminate form must be REWRITTEN into one of them.
0·∞ becomes a quotient by pushing one factor downstairs; 1^∞ yields to logarithms.
ln x ≪ any power of x ≪ eˣ — and L'Hôpital is what proves the hierarchy.
steps.teaser: That is what derivatives are FOR. Next course: what integrals are for — areas, volumes, and average values.

concept.body: L'Hôpital needs a fraction. If you have a product, push one factor downstairs as its reciprocal. If you have a difference, put it over a common denominator. Manufacture the quotient FIRST, then check the form.

explanationVariants: x·ln x becomes (ln x)/(1/x) — the x has moved downstairs as 1/x.
Any factor can go to the denominator by taking its reciprocal.

widget.prompt: Rewrite x·ln x as a quotient.

options.label: (ln x)/(1/x)
options.feedback: Right — the x moves downstairs as its reciprocal, and the product becomes a quotient.

options.label: (1/x)/(ln x)
options.feedback: That inverts the whole expression and changes the limit entirely. Keep ln x on top and move the x down.
